Is Egypt Safe to Visit? An Honest Answer From the People Who Guide There

What UK, US, German and French travel advice says about Egypt, including the Western Desert, which areas are restricted, and what private travel does and does not change

21 November 2026 · 14 minute read

By Islam Hussein, Sillage Égypte journey designer. Last updated: November 2026.

Quick answer: For the Egypt most visitors see, the answer is a qualified yes, and no government can promise more than that. As of 6 November 2026, the UK, US and German advisories do not advise against travel to Cairo and Giza, Luxor, Aswan, Abu Simbel, Alexandria or the Red Sea resorts. They do advise against North Sinai and the desert borders, the US lists the whole Western Desert as Do Not Travel, which covers our White Desert experience and Beyond the Nile, and the UK and US warn of a real, nationwide terrorism risk and of regional tension that can disrupt flights. Private travel does not change that risk, but it removes much of the daily friction: you are met inside the airport, you have your own car and Egyptologist, and our team is reachable at any hour.

"Is Egypt safe?" reaches our journey designers more often than any other question, and it usually arrives with a trip already half-formed in it: the traveller has imagined the early hour at the Valley of the Kings or the boat at dusk, and then remembered a headline. A fair answer has to untangle three things: what governments actually advise today, which areas their warnings cover (and which they pointedly do not), and what safety means day to day on the ground. That is this post. Sillage Égypte (sillage-egypte.com), the private Egypt journey designer, writes from inside the country, and honest counsel about risk is part of the service.

Is Egypt safe right now? The short answer

For the Nile Valley, Cairo and the coast, the official position today is "open, with caution", not "avoid". The Western Desert is the exception, covered below. As of 6 November 2026 the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) advises against all travel to parts of Egypt, but names North Sinai and the strip within 20 km of the Libyan border, not Cairo, the Nile Valley, Abu Simbel or the Red Sea resorts. The US State Department lists Egypt at Level 2 ("Exercise Increased Caution"). Germany's Foreign Office publishes a partial travel warning for North Sinai, the Israeli border area and remote parts of the Sahara.

That is not the same as "no risk", and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something. The FCDO says plainly that terrorists are likely to try to carry out attacks in Egypt, that attacks could be indiscriminate, and that they could take place in places visited by foreigners. Germany describes the overall situation as stable and calm but still lists a nationwide terrorism risk. And since early 2026 every government has added a paragraph on regional tension: on 27 October 2026 the FCDO updated its wording for the whole Middle East, describing the context as "deeply unpredictable" with a high risk of sudden escalation, and warning of possible airspace closures, flight cancellations and extra security checks.

The risks that most often touch travellers are far more ordinary: Cairo traffic, summer heat, touts, and the persistent attention reserved for anyone visibly new. Those are manageable, and that is where private travel does its quiet work.

Counsel, given honestly. If a phrase such as "exercise increased caution" would shadow your holiday, Egypt may keep you slightly on edge: checkpoints and bag scanners are part of the landscape here. And when a traveller or a season is simply wrong for Egypt, we say so, a habit explained in why we will sometimes talk you out of a trip. If the worry underneath is really about timing, start with our guide to when to go to Egypt.

What official travel advice says

Editorial snapshot dated 6 November 2026, from the sources linked below. Advice changes without ceremony, sometimes for regional politics rather than events on the ground, so re-read your own government's page in the week you book.

Advisory Overall position Advises against
UK: FCDO Egypt travel advice (main page updated 27 October 2026) Advises against all travel to parts of Egypt only; none of the main tourist areas is named All travel: North Sinai Governorate; within 20 km of the Libya border (except El Salloum, where the advice is all but essential). All but essential: northern South Sinai beyond the St Catherine to Nuweiba road (coastal areas excepted); east of the Suez Canal in Ismailiya; the Western Desert west of the Nile Valley and Delta, with listed exceptions; the Hala'ib Triangle and Bir Tawil Trapezoid
US: State Department Egypt advisory Reported at Level 2 of 4: Exercise Increased Caution (Embassy Cairo guidance, March 2026) Do not travel: Northern and Middle Sinai, the Western Desert and border areas. Our White Desert experience and Beyond the Nile fall in that region
Germany: Auswärtiges Amt, Ägypten (Stand 6 November 2026) Partial travel warning (Teilreisewarnung) North Sinai and the Egyptian-Israeli border zone (except the immediate coast and Taba); remote parts of the Sahara, including the border zones with Libya and Sudan. In southern Sinai it advises against unaccompanied individual excursions and overland drives
France: France Diplomatie, Égypte (security section dated 21 September 2026) Red zone limited to the areas below Formally advised against: the Israel border zone and North Sinai

The UK's Western Desert wording deserves a close read, because our desert days fall under it. The FCDO advises against all but essential travel across the Western Desert, then lists exceptions that include Luxor, Qina, Aswan, Abu Simbel and the Valley of the Kings, Faiyum, Siwa town, the Marsa Matruh to Siwa road, the White Desert and Black Desert, and the oasis towns of Bahariya, Farafra, Dakhla and Kharga. The Bahariya to Siwa road stays under the all-but-essential advice: the FCDO says it is closed and there are military checkpoints. For Bahariya, Farafra and the White and Black Deserts, the FCDO says visitors must apply for permits in advance and use an official guide.

The US goes further. Its official Egypt travel advisory, checked on 6 November 2026, says not to travel to the Western Desert, and we read that as covering our White Desert experience and Beyond the Nile. If you are travelling on US advice, or with US insurance, take that seriously: the UK's exceptions do not cancel it. Germany warns against remote parts of the Sahara and says remote desert areas need a special permit and a tour through an operator recognised by the tourism ministry, and that the authorities can cancel even approved desert trips at short notice.

One more point from the FCDO matters for anyone relying on insurance: travel insurance could be invalidated if you travel against FCDO advice. Comprehensive travel insurance is a condition of booking with us, and we check your plans against official advice when we design the journey. Your own government's advice and your own policy decide what you are covered for, so ask your insurer about any desert day in writing.

Which areas are actually restricted?

The restricted areas fall into a few groups. Most lie nowhere near a Sillage journey; the Western Desert is the one that needs a straight answer.

  1. North Sinai Governorate. Advised against by the UK, the US, Germany and France. No site on our journeys lies within it.
  2. The Libya border. The FCDO draws its line at 20 km; Germany warns against remote Sahara areas, including the Libya and Sudan border zones. The UK also advises against all but essential travel to the Hala'ib Triangle and Bir Tawil Trapezoid.
  3. The Israeli border. Germany and France both mark the border zone, Germany excepting the immediate coast and Taba.
  4. The Western Desert. The UK advises against all but essential travel, with the exceptions above, which cover the oasis towns and the White Desert and Black Desert. The US says do not travel to the region. Our White Desert experience and Beyond the Nile are in it.
  5. Northern South Sinai (partial). The FCDO advises against all but essential travel beyond the St Catherine to Nuweiba road, except coastal areas. Germany does not issue a full warning for Sharm el-Sheikh, Dahab and Nuweiba but advises against unaccompanied individual excursions and overland drives. We do not place St Catherine's Monastery and Mount Sinai on one side of the FCDO line or the other here, and we do not currently sell Sinai excursions; check the current wording before booking one elsewhere.

Siwa Oasis sits nearer the Libyan frontier than anywhere else we travel. The FCDO lists Siwa town and the Marsa Matruh to Siwa road among its exceptions, and Beyond the Nile travels to Siwa and back along the coast, not on the closed Bahariya to Siwa road.

Everyday safety: what actually touches travellers

In day-to-day experience, Egypt's tourist areas are heavily policed, and the things most likely to affect a visitor are traffic, heat and touts. The FCDO describes the crime rate as generally low, with pickpocketing rare, and asks visitors to take the same sensible precautions they would at home. If you need the tourist police, the number is 126; the FCDO adds that a crime not reported before you leave Egypt is difficult to prosecute later.

Security is visible by design: officers at major sites, checkpoints on approach roads, and bag screening at many hotels and museums. The intensity varies by site, and some visitors find the presence heavy. It is there to keep the sites orderly.

The rest is ordinary travel sense, Egyptian edition:

  • Traffic. Cairo drives loudly and with conviction; crossing a boulevard is a genuine local skill. Walk beside your guide, or let the car do the crossing for you.
  • Heat and water. Luxor passes 40 °C in summer, and museum hours exist for a reason. Carry water, drink bottled, and keep the middle of the day soft.
  • Touts and scams. The "free" photograph, the helpful stranger at the gate, the unsolicited direction that ends at a shop. The FCDO warns that scammers and touts sometimes target foreign nationals in tourist areas, and notes you do not need to buy a visa from an airport agent. A polite no through your Egyptologist ends the exchange.
  • Dress and attention. Shoulders and knees covered for mosques and churches. Attention in the street is common and wearing; modest dress and firm courtesy blunt most of it, and company changes the day materially.
  • Swimming. Germany warns of bilharzia in fresh water in the Nile Delta and Valley. Keep to the hotel pool.

A few notes from the ground:

  • Checkpoints on the desert roads are a routine part of driving in Egypt.
  • The most useful safety device in Egypt is a local number that answers. Ours is the guide beside you, and behind the guide a team reachable at any hour of the journey.
  • Walk with an Egyptian colleague and the character of a street changes: the offers fall away, and the questions turn from transactions to football and pharaohs.

How private travel helps, without pretending it changes everything

Private travel does not alter a country's risk profile, and no honest journey designer would claim otherwise. What it changes is your exposure to the small risks and your speed of help when anything goes wrong. The shape of a private arrival shows it:

  1. The entry visa is arranged and included, so you are not buying one from an agent in the arrivals hall.
  2. You are met inside the terminal, before taxis, touts or ticket machines get a turn at you.
  3. A private car, not a rotation of taxis negotiated one by one.
  4. Your own certified Egyptologist from the first day to the last, accountable to you alone.
  5. A team reachable at any hour stands behind both, with the standing of the operator behind Sillage Égypte, Capital Travel Service (Ministry of Tourism licence 2179, ETAA member), to rearrange a flight, a boat or a day.

What private travel is not: a force field. It will not remove the terrorism risk the FCDO describes, lower the temperature at Karnak in August, or thin a viewpoint the whole world has come to stand on, though private hours and permits can come close. A journey such as The Complete Egypt, thirteen days with five nights on a private dahabiya between Esna and Aswan, from €7,500 per person for two or more travellers, runs on exactly this chain from arrival to departure. Comprehensive travel insurance is a condition of booking, written into our terms rather than suggested; and if a journey is wrong for you (wrong season, wrong shape, wrong year) our counsel will say so before any deposit is mentioned.

FAQ

Is Egypt safe to visit right now? For the main tourist areas, the UK, US and German advisories do not advise against travel, as of 6 November 2026, but all three flag a terrorism risk and regional tension, and all three advise against North Sinai and the border zones. The US is also reported to say do not travel to the Western Desert, which includes our White Desert experience and Beyond the Nile. No destination is risk-free. Read your own government's advice in the week you book, and make sure your insurance covers the journey.

Is Egypt safe for European travellers? The German and French advisories, the pages most European guests read first, take the same line as the British and American ones: warnings for North Sinai and the border areas, and caution rather than avoidance elsewhere. Germany adds a nationwide terrorism risk and a note that flight restrictions are possible given the situation in the Gulf. Nothing in the advisories singles out European visitors.

Is Egypt safe for families with children? Many families travel to Egypt, within the travelled areas and with the adjustments children need anywhere warm and busy: water, shade, midday rest and a slower pace. A private journey suits this well: the car is yours, the day flexes, and your Egyptologist can choose the sites that hold a child's attention.

Is Sharm el-Sheikh safe? What about the rest of Sinai? Sharm el-Sheikh is not among the areas the UK or US advise against, but Sinai is where the advice is most detailed. The FCDO advises against all but essential travel in northern South Sinai beyond the St Catherine to Nuweiba road, and Germany advises against unaccompanied individual excursions and overland drives in the south. Sharm is usually reached by air (our Sharm el-Sheikh guide covers it in full). We do not currently sell Sinai excursions; re-read the current wording before booking a Mount Sinai climb elsewhere.

Is a private tour safer than a group tour in Egypt? Group coaches also travel in Egypt's tourist areas; this is not a choice between safe and unsafe. A private tour removes variables: a private car rather than a rotation, one accountable Egyptologist, no taxis negotiated, hours chosen against the crowds, and a single phone call that reaches your own team. The gain is as much calm and resilience as safety.

Is Egypt safe for a woman travelling alone? Many women do it, with care. The FCDO advises female travellers to take caution when travelling alone, particularly at night and in taxis, and notes that most reported sexual assaults occurred in Red Sea resorts, often involving someone the victim had already met, including hotel and excursion staff. Attention in the street is real and tiring; modest dress and firm courtesy blunt most of it. A woman travelling alone with us has a private Egyptologist and driver, walking the sites in company rather than alone, and a female guide is available on request.

What happens if something goes wrong mid-journey? You make one call. The team behind the journey is reachable at any hour, and the operator behind Sillage Égypte, Capital Travel Service (Ministry of Tourism licence 2179, ETAA member), is an Egyptian company with the standing to rearrange a boat, a flight or a day. Comprehensive travel insurance is a condition of booking. Most "emergencies" turn out to be a changed flight or a heat headache; all of them are met by people who already know your journey.

The takeaway

Egypt's main tourist areas are open and, as of 6 November 2026, not subject to advice against travel from the UK, US or Germany, but the same advisories describe a real terrorism risk and a tense region, and they restrict North Sinai and the borderlands. The Western Desert is where advice divides, and our desert days sit in it, so read your own government's page and your policy before choosing them. What you will most often meet is traffic, heat and touts, and a journey designed privately absorbs most of all three.
